person.name: Yusuf Wadi
person.tagline: Engineer. Artist. Curious about how minds compute.

items.title: TinyNeRF and Instant-NGP in tinygrad
items.summary: I reimplemented TinyNeRF and Instant-NGP's multiresolution hash encoding inside tinygrad, a minimal deep-learning framework.
items.body:
I wanted to understand NeRF below the level of a library call, so I rebuilt it in tinygrad. The model has per-level hash tables with spatial hashing, density and color MLPs, positional encoding, volume rendering and LAMB optimization, with a JIT-compiled render path.

tinygrad was missing several ops I needed, so I wrote them: a 5-D bilinear `grid_sample`, `roll`, an exclusive `cumprod` and `meshgrid`, plus a small data loader.

TinyNeRF trained and rendered novel views, and the Instant-NGP model ran end to end on synthetic data. It pairs with my ACM NeRF benchmarking study.

items.title: FlowState
items.summary: A real-time brain-computer interface that uses EEG alpha-band power as an attention signal to speed up or slow down video playback.
items.body:
FlowState reads EEG from a Muse headband over Lab Streaming Layer and computes alpha-band power as a rough attention signal. When attention drops, YouTube playback speeds up or slows down in response.

It is a proof of concept, not a product: a signal from a head, a bit of signal processing, and something you can see change on a screen.

items.title: mtg-vector-math
items.summary: Distilled card embeddings for Magic: The Gathering, small enough to run as pure numpy on a serverless function.
items.body:
A bge-small teacher model produces 105-dimensional soft labels for cards. A TF-IDF plus two-layer MLP student learns to match them, so inference needs only numpy: roughly 2 to 5 MB of weights and a cold start under 100 ms on Vercel.

I checked that the embedding space still behaves like one by running analogy tests in the king/queen style on card concepts. The point was to see how much of a large model's structure a tiny model can keep, and to ship it somewhere cheap.

items.title: mtg-oracle
items.summary: A Magic: The Gathering deck-matching engine with TF-IDF, keyword and hybrid scoring, running live on Vercel.
items.body:
mtg-oracle matches a player's cards to decks using TF-IDF cosine similarity, keyword matching, and a hybrid of the two, with penalties that account for prerequisites a deck needs. It runs as a Python serverless API on Vercel, and a monthly GitHub Actions job refreshes the card data.

I designed the scoring approach and the architecture and built it with AI-assisted tooling, which is how I ship working products quickly. The design decisions are mine; the interesting part was deciding what "a good match" should mean.

items.title: chess_vis
items.summary: A Python visualizer that shows which squares are contested in a chess position.
items.body:
chess_vis takes a position in FEN notation and draws which squares each side attacks, so contested squares stand out. It is written by hand in object-oriented Python.

I built it while mentoring at a chess club, as a teaching aid: it is easier to explain why a square matters when you can see both sides pressing on it.

items.title: freaqy
items.summary: A machine-learning mean-reversion trading research system built on Freqtrade and FreqAI, with 105 strategy versions.
items.body:
freaqy is crypto trading research on 5.5 years of 15-minute, 1-hour and 4-hour data across 14 pairs. I went through 105 strategy versions: rule-based z-score mean reversion first, then ML with LightGBM and XGBoost, and a stacking ensemble that requires models to agree. The training target is z-score reversion rather than noisy raw returns, and circuit breakers (daily loss limit, loss cooldown, volatility gate) sit outside the model.

The most useful lesson was about honesty in backtests. I overfit badly at first (402 features on 557 samples), rebuilt with 31 hand-picked features, and showed that fee assumptions alone can flip a strategy from profit to loss.

items.title: TheraPT / mun-ching
items.summary: An LLM therapy chatbot, and my first time fine-tuning a language model.
items.body:
I fine-tuned GPT-3 first on synthetic therapist and client dialogues, then on about 200,000 lines of therapy transcripts, working with a partner who studies cognitive science. On noisy transcribed speech, prompt engineering beat fine-tuning.

We added conversation memory and a Tkinter interface, then moved to a Vue/Nuxt web app deployed on Linode. It was my way into fine-tuning.

items.title: PowerSlides
items.summary: A Streamlit app that turns a prompt or text into a PowerPoint deck.
items.body:
PowerSlides uses an LLM and Pandoc to generate `.pptx` decks from a prompt or pasted text. It is Dockerized and was publicly hosted for a time on Google Cloud.

It is fun and very useful, and it is where I settled on Streamlit as my favorite frontend framework for getting a Python idea in front of people quickly.

items.title: autoApply
items.summary: A Selenium and BeautifulSoup script that automates filling in applications on Greenhouse job boards.
items.body: autoApply was my introduction to web scraping and browser automation. It drives a browser with Selenium, reads pages with BeautifulSoup, and fills in applications on Greenhouse-hosted job boards.

items.title: camper_registry
items.summary: A QR-code attendance system I built for a summer camp.
items.body: A summer camp needed attendance for about 50 campers, so I built a QR-code attendance system for it.

items.title: Lumii
items.summary: A modular on-device voice therapy assistant tuned for the Raspberry Pi 5.
items.body: Lumii runs entirely on a Raspberry Pi 5 (ARM64). Audio streams through callbacks, voice activity detection is JIT-compiled with Numba, Whisper handles speech-to-text, VADER scores emotion, and a local LLM runs through Ollama. Replies are spoken with ElevenLabs, and a safety layer filters crisis terms. Multiprocessing uses CPU affinity tuning.

items.title: PMSI: predictive maintenance
items.summary: A Toyota hackathon project: unsupervised anomaly detection over vehicle telemetry with subsystem-level fault attribution.
items.body:
I was the sole author of the ML inference server for PMSI, a team entry in an internal Toyota hackathon. The data was about 7 GB of CAN telemetry from 51 vehicles, with no failure labels, so the model had to be unsupervised.

I built a PCA baseline and a PyTorch masked autoencoder and combined them into a hybrid detector. Per-feature reconstruction error gives both an anomaly score and the subsystem likely at fault. On a synthetic fault-injection test, brake and engine faults were detected about 100% of the time. The scorer is a stateless FastAPI service with weights exported to numpy, so it runs without torch on an AWS Lambda container.

items.title: Toyota: Apple Maps EV routing
items.summary: I led the backend for Toyota's integration with Apple Maps EV routing on CarPlay, from proof of concept to production.
items.body:
I am a Software Engineer at Toyota Motor North America (Oct 2024 to present). I led Toyota's Apple Maps EV routing integration on CarPlay from proof of concept to production in about 5 months. It is live in 3 AWS regions and streams over a million vehicle records a day from thousands of Toyota EVs.

The backend is Go on AWS EKS. A fault-tolerant Kinesis consumer uses concurrent shard workers, a circuit breaker and exponential backoff, and writes with idempotent atomic MongoDB upserts, which removed duplicate records. A low-latency REST API with Datadog tracing and structured logging serves single-digit-millisecond p95 latency in-service, far under its 200 ms SLO, and stays above its 99.5% success target.

I also authored physics-based EV consumption and DC fast-charging models in Apple's EV portal, validated against real test-drive traces to about 1% mean state-of-charge error.

items.title: Toyota: home energy management (HEMS)
items.summary: I build Go microservices for Toyota's home EV-charging platform.
items.body:
HEMS is Toyota's home EV-charging platform. I built Go microservices for it, including an OCPP 2.1 WebSocket gateway with mTLS (Security Profile 3) and Kafka message streaming, plus boot and event services for charger telemetry and V2H backup-power events.

I also redesigned firmware distribution from an always-on EKS service to event-driven AWS Lambda and Step Functions, so a twice-a-year workload does not need an always-on service. I built the signing workflow with mTLS OAuth, async callbacks and LocalStack-based testing.

items.title: Toyota: charging-station data health
items.summary: A data-quality pipeline and dashboard over more than 100,000 EV charging-station records from five provider networks.
items.body: I built a geospatial data-quality pipeline and a Streamlit dashboard over 100,000+ EV charging-station records from 5 provider networks. It surfaces stale, missing and inconsistent station data, and coverage gaps, sometimes called charging deserts.

items.title: Toyota: competitive teardown
items.summary: I led a teardown of Tesla's app ecosystem and presented the findings to Toyota Motor Corporation executives.
items.body: I led a competitive teardown of Tesla's app ecosystem, comparing 110 app frameworks against 10, and presented the findings to Toyota Motor Corporation executives.

items.title: Seeloz: Data Science Intern
items.summary: A summer at an AI supply-chain startup working on reinforcement-learning simulation and a data-pipeline port.
items.body:
Seeloz is an AI inventory-optimization startup in Dallas. I developed a reinforcement-learning simulation of client inventory, covering finished and semi-finished goods, to optimize surplus, using Ray RLlib.

I also ported stages of a Scala/Spark SAP ETL pipeline to SQL and led the investigation into why SQL and Scala inventory numbers diverged (date ranges, currency conversion, over-delivery adjustments). When the company lost its Azure SQL connection mid-project, I proposed and built a self-instantiating SQL Server database in Docker from client CSV files. It unblocked me and one other intern within a week.

items.title: Monoware Studios: Full-Stack Developer Intern
items.summary: Two summers building web apps, and a retrieval-augmented chatbot for company documents.
items.body:
I interned at Monoware Studios in Richardson, TX across two summers. In 2022 I started with a small onboarding project and then built web apps and a front end for a new-initiative prototype, using Vue, Nuxt and Tailwind CSS.

In 2023 I built a retrieval-augmented generation chatbot with LangChain and Pinecone, with a Nuxt/Vue web component, for searching internal company documents and FAQs. I do not know what became of it after I left, so I make no claim about its use.

items.title: Decoding joystick movement from ECoG
items.summary: I co-led a Neuromatch Academy project that predicts continuous joystick trajectories from electrocorticography recordings.
items.body:
As research co-lead at Neuromatch Academy, I built a brain-computer-interface decoding pipeline that predicts continuous joystick cursor trajectories from ECoG recordings. I trained PyTorch autoencoders for feature extraction, including a smoothness-regularized LSTM autoencoder, and LSTMs for time-series decoding, and also tried CNN and Transformer decoders. Test RMSE was 0.094 on 855 held-out samples.

Half the team dropped out partway through. I re-scoped the project with my remaining teammate and later brought a returning member back in as presentation lead. We presented to the cohort, and the work was published on Neuromatch's site. This is my favorite project.

items.title: Measuring immersion in NeRFs
items.summary: As research lead at ACM Research UTD, I helped benchmark four NeRF methods on 26 datasets for VR use.
items.body:
The study compared NeRF, Mip-NeRF, Nerfacto and Instant-NGP, trained through nerfstudio on 26 datasets. Eighteen were captured by our team (6 scenes with 3 capture methods: Insta360 One RS, Insta360 360 and iPhone 12 Pro, processed with COLMAP or Polycam) and 8 came from the original NeRF paper. Most training ran on an RTX 3090.

We measured train time, memory, storage, GPU usage, loss and accuracy against real data. NeRF and Mip-NeRF took up to about two days to train, while Nerfacto and Instant-NGP took minutes. I owned the Instant-NGP track, ran training and the test suite myself, and proposed the comparative-analysis framing that settled a disagreement about direction. The poster was titled "Measuring Immersion in Neural Radiance Fields."

items.title: Neuromatch computational neuroscience program and certificate
items.summary: A 128-hour Computational Neuroscience certificate from Neuromatch Academy, July 2024.
items.body: I completed Neuromatch Academy's Computational Neuroscience program, 128 hours in July 2024, and earned the certificate. It covers neural modeling, machine learning for neural data and causal inference, and ends in a team research project, which for me was the ECoG joystick decoding work.

items.title: Liminal Bevy
items.summary: A passion project: a first-person generator of procedural liminal spaces in Rust with Bevy and WGSL, and my first large project built with agentic workflows.
items.body:
Liminal Bevy is a passion project, and the first large-scale project I have built with agentic workflows. I directed the design and the system, and most of the code was written by AI agents.

The game grows corridors and rooms from a relational grammar defined in an editable RON recipe. Recipes can be mutated and crossed over, and walkability and seam invariants are checked before one world replaces another, so the player never steps into a broken space.

items.title: Rarephish
items.summary: A seeded procedural idle fishing game with generative fish, first in Unity and later in Rust.
items.body:
Rarephish started in C# and Unity and moved to Rust and Bevy in 2026. Worlds are deterministic, built from a seeded ChaCha8 random number generator, and each fish is generated rather than hand-drawn, so a seed always reproduces the same pond.

The interesting problem is making generated things feel individual: small rules for shape, color and rarity that combine into something you want to collect.

items.title: VR modding
items.summary: Years of Unity modding for VR games, with Blender and 3D printing alongside.
items.body:
I made Unity mods for Blade & Sorcery and Risk of Rain 2, and used Blender for models and 3D printing to bring some of them into physical form.

This is where I learned to work inside a large game I did not write: reading how it fits together, adding to it without breaking it, and making a thing someone else will play.

items.title: TiltShift
items.summary: A concept prototype for converting 2D photos and video into 3D using monocular depth estimation.
items.body:
TiltShift is a concept and prototype for turning flat photos and video into 3D scenes with monocular depth estimation. I explored Depth Pro, MiDaS and TMPI.

It is not a finished tool.

items.title: Skills
items.summary: The languages and tools I use most, grouped by how much I have shipped with them.
items.body:
**Daily and in production:** Go and Python, on AWS (EKS, Lambda, Step Functions, S3, API Gateway), with MongoDB, Docker, Kubernetes, Datadog and REST/OpenAPI services.

**Proficient:** TypeScript and JavaScript, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, Kinesis, and the Python web and visualization stack (FastAPI, Flask, Streamlit, Plotly).

**Machine learning:** PyTorch, scikit-learn, pandas and NumPy, LightGBM and XGBoost, plus LLM work with fine-tuning, RAG and local models through Ollama. Anomaly detection, autoencoders and time-series modeling are the areas I know best.

**Familiar or growing:** Rust, Swift, Kafka, Spark, Unity and Bevy. I use agentic coding tools daily.

items.title: IMC Prosperity and Optiver Ready Trader Go
items.summary: Trading competitions where I led small teams; 50th of 10,000 in IMC Prosperity.
items.body:
In IMC Prosperity 2024 I was research lead of a three-person team writing market-making and mean-reversion strategies, and we placed 50th of 10,000, the top 0.5%. In Optiver's Ready Trader Go (March 2023) I led a three-person team building low-latency trading algorithms in Python and C++.

Both used the same method: a custom market simulator and Bayesian parameter search with Hyperopt, parallelized on Apache Spark for about a 9x speedup.

items.title: B.S. Computer Science, UT Dallas
items.summary: A computer science degree with coursework in machine learning, AI, databases, operating systems and algorithms.
items.body:
I studied computer science at the University of Texas at Dallas, graduating in December 2023. Coursework included machine learning, artificial intelligence, data science methods, databases, automata theory, advanced data structures and algorithms, operating systems and computer architecture.

My senior design project, Raybender, was a Swift macOS command launcher built with a team of three, in which I was the top contributor. I was in ACM Research, the Data Science Club and the Japanese Language Association.

items.body: I speak English natively and Arabic fluently. My Japanese and Spanish are basic; the Japanese is from the Japanese language club at university.
